questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has 3 weeks of a puffy face in the mornings, swollen legs and frothy urine. She has gained 5 kg. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her JVP is not raised and her chest is clear. She has pitting oedema to the thighs. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Heavy proteinuria with low albumin, high cholesterol and generalised oedema is nephrotic syndrome. Nephritic syndrome gives haematuria and hypertension instead.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Periorbital oedema, **frothy urine** and heavy **proteinuria** with a normal JVP point to a renal protein leak, not a cardiac cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Nephrotic syndrome: proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia and oedema.

elim: Expect haematuria, hypertension and oliguria; her dipstick has no blood and BP is normal.
Her JVP is not raised and her chest is clear; heart failure does not cause 4+ proteinuria.
Low albumin from cirrhosis does not cause heavy proteinuria or frothy urine.
Albumin is lost in the gut, so the urine would not show 4+ protein.

steps.x: **D. Nephrotic syndrome.** Proteinuria + hypoalbuminaemia + hyperlipidaemia + oedema = nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has had type 2 diabetes for 22 years with background retinopathy. He has 2 months of ankle swelling. His BP is 148/88 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Investigations show urine protein:creatinine ratio 480 mg/mmol (<15) and serum albumin 23 g/L (35–50). His HbA1c is 71 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his nephrotic syndrome?
questions.e: Long-standing diabetes with retinopathy and heavy proteinuria makes diabetic nephropathy the likely secondary cause. IgA nephropathy presents with haematuria.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Long-standing **diabetes** with other microvascular disease (**retinopathy**) is a common secondary cause in adults.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Diabetic nephropathy.

elim: Usually causes visible haematuria after a sore throat, not bland heavy proteinuria.
The classic cause in children, not in a man with long-standing diabetes and retinopathy.
A nephritic picture with haematuria after a streptococcal infection.
Causes hypertension and a rise in creatinine, not nephrotic-range proteinuria.

steps.x: **A. Diabetic nephropathy.** Diabetes is a common secondary cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, especially with retinopathy.

questions.stem: A 46 year old builder has had 6 weeks of leg swelling and frothy urine. He has taken naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 9 months for back pain. He has no rash, joint pain or diabetes. His BP is 128/80 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. His serum albumin is 20 g/L (35–50).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his nephrotic syndrome?
questions.e: Regular naproxen is a recognised secondary cause of nephrotic syndrome; stopping it is part of treating the cause. He has no features of lupus or diabetes.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 9 months
no rash, joint pain or diabetes
steps.x: A drug history of **regular NSAID** use with no lupus or diabetes points to a drug cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Regular NSAID (naproxen) use.

elim: Possible in chronic inflammation, but there is no long-standing inflammatory disease here.
An infectious cause, but nothing in the history suggests it.
He has no rash or joint pain.
He has no diabetes.

steps.x: **C. Regular NSAID use.** Always take a drug history: regular NSAIDs can cause nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has 4 weeks of swollen ankles and frothy urine. She has had painful wrists, mouth ulcers and a rash across her cheeks that is worse in the sun. Her BP is 132/84 mmHg. Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 390 mg/mmol (<15). Renal biopsy shows thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial immune complex deposits.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: A malar rash, arthralgia and mouth ulcers with membranous change on biopsy (GBM thickening, subepithelial deposits) points to lupus. HIV is linked to FSGS.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: rash across her cheeks that is worse in the sun
steps.x: A **photosensitive malar rash**, mouth ulcers and arthritis are lupus; the biopsy shows **membranous** nephropathy, which is associated with SLE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: SLE causing membranous nephropathy.

elim: No history of diabetes, and diabetic changes are not subepithelial immune deposits.
HIV classically causes FSGS, not membranous change.
Biopsy would show no immune complex deposits.
Causes a nephritic picture after a throat infection.

steps.x: **E. Systemic lupus erythematosus.** Membranous nephropathy is associated with SLE: look for the rash, joints and ulcers.

questions.stem: A 59 year old White man has nephrotic syndrome. He has no diabetes, rash or joint pains and takes no regular medicines. His BP is 136/82 mmHg. Investigations show serum albumin 21 g/L (35–50), urine protein:creatinine ratio 640 mg/mmol (<15) and positive anti-PLA2R antibodies. A renal biopsy is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?
o: GBM thickening with subepithelial immune deposits
questions.e: Anti-PLA2R antibodies mean membranous nephropathy: GBM thickening with subepithelial immune complex deposits. Normal light microscopy fits minimal change disease.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: no diabetes, rash or joint pains
steps.x: **Anti-PLA2R** in an adult with primary nephrotic syndrome is membranous nephropathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thickened GBM with subepithelial immune complexes.

elim: Seen in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, not membranous nephropathy.
Nodular glomerulosclerosis of diabetic nephropathy; he is not diabetic.
IgA nephropathy, which presents with haematuria.
Typical of minimal change disease, which has no immune complex deposits.

steps.x: **B. GBM thickening with subepithelial immune deposits.** Anti-PLA2R = membranous = thick GBM + subepithelial deposits.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with nephrotic syndrome has routine thyroid function tests. She has no symptoms of thyroid disease and no goitre. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm. Investigations show TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 14 pmol/L (10–22) and total T4 42 nmol/L (60–150). Her serum albumin is 18 g/L (35–50).
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her thyroid results?
questions.e: In nephrotic syndrome, thyroid-binding globulin is lost in the urine, lowering total T4 while free T4 and TSH stay normal. She is euthyroid.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Only the **total T4** is low; **free T4 and TSH are normal**, so the problem is the carrier protein, not the gland.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Binding protein lost in urine.

elim: Would raise TSH and lower free T4; both are normal.
Free T4 would be low with an inappropriately low TSH.
Occurs in acute severe illness; she is well.
Means a raised TSH with normal free T4; her TSH is normal.

steps.x: **E. Urinary loss of thyroid-binding globulin.** Low total T4 with normal free T4 and TSH in nephrotic syndrome = urinary loss of thyroid-binding globulin.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with nephrotic syndrome has 2 weeks of gradually increasing breathlessness on exertion. He has no chest pain or haemoptysis. His pulse rate is 82 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There is stony dullness and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral blunting of the costophrenic angles with meniscus: bilateral pleural effusions.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
o: Pleural effusions from low oncotic pressure
questions.e: Gradual breathlessness with bilateral stony dullness and effusions on X-ray are transudates from low albumin. Sudden breathlessness would instead raise concern for PE.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: stony dullness and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases
steps.x: **Gradual** onset with **bilateral stony dullness** means fluid: transudative effusions from hypoalbuminaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Transudative pleural effusions.

elim: He has no fever or cough, and consolidation is not stony dull.
Gives sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain, not gradual onset with bilateral stony dullness.
Gives fine crackles, not stony dullness, and develops over months.
Would expect a raised JVP and crackles, not bilateral stony dullness alone.

steps.x: **B. Pleural effusions from low oncotic pressure.** Low albumin lowers oncotic pressure: effusions, ascites and oedema. Sudden breathlessness is PE until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 57 year old White man has 2 months of progressive ankle swelling and frothy urine. He has no diabetes, takes no regular medicines and has no rash, joint pains or recent infections. His BP is 134/80 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. His serum albumin is 19 g/L (35–50) and HIV test is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological cause?
questions.e: In White adults with no secondary cause, membranous nephropathy is the most common cause, followed by FSGS. Minimal change disease is the children's cause.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: no diabetes, takes no regular medicines
steps.x: An **adult** with primary nephrotic syndrome and no secondary cause: think of the commonest adult cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Membranous nephropathy.

elim: The second most common primary cause in adults; most often linked to HIV, which is negative here.
Presents with haematuria, not bland nephrotic syndrome.
The most common cause in children, not White adults.
A nephritic syndrome after a throat infection.

steps.x: **C. Membranous nephropathy.** Children: minimal change. White adults: membranous, then FSGS.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy is brought in with swollen eyelids and a swollen scrotum for 5 days. He had a runny nose and cough 2 weeks ago. His BP is 96/60 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. His serum albumin is 15 g/L (35–50). He goes into remission with oral prednisolone.
questions.q: Which would be the most likely finding if a renal biopsy were performed?
o: Normal light microscopy with podocyte foot process effacement
questions.e: A young child after a viral URTI with steroid response has minimal change disease: normal light microscopy, foot process effacement on electron microscopy and no immune complexes.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: runny nose and cough 2 weeks ago
steps.x: A **young child** after a **viral URTI** who responds to **steroids** has minimal change disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Minimal change: normal light microscopy, effacement on electron microscopy.

elim: Seen in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with acute kidney injury.
FSGS, which is less common and usually steroid-resistant.
Seen in lupus and nephritic patterns, not minimal change disease.
Membranous nephropathy, the commonest adult cause.

steps.x: **B. Normal light microscopy with podocyte foot process effacement.** Minimal change disease: podocyte foot process effacement with no immune complex deposition.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man with membranous nephropathy has 6 hours of severe constant left flank pain and dark red urine. He also feels short of breath. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 138/86 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. His creatinine has risen from 88 to 162 µmol/L. Ultrasound shows an enlarged left kidney.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Flank pain, haematuria, an enlarged kidney and rising creatinine in membranous nephropathy is renal vein thrombosis, from a hypercoagulable state. Breathlessness raises concern for embolism.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Constant flank pain** with **haematuria** and an **enlarged kidney** in membranous nephropathy is a venous clot.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Renal vein thrombosis.

elim: Would expect fever, rigors and pyuria.
Does not develop over hours with a sudden rise in creatinine.
Arterial; there is no AF or embolic source, and nephrotic patients clot in the veins.
Pain is colicky loin to groin, and the kidney is not enlarged.

steps.x: **D. Renal vein thrombosis.** Membranous nephropathy + flank pain + haematuria = renal vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has 3 weeks of swollen legs. She has noticed her urine looks foamy in the toilet. Her BP is 126/78 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Her serum albumin is 19 g/L (35–50) and cholesterol 8.9 mmol/L (<5.0). Urine microscopy is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on urine microscopy?
questions.e: Nephrotic syndrome causes lipiduria, seen as oval fat bodies and fatty casts. Red cell casts indicate nephritic syndrome.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Heavy proteinuria with **hyperlipidaemia** and no blood means a nephrotic sediment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lipiduria.

elim: Seen in acute tubular necrosis.
Glomerular bleeding in nephritic syndrome; her dipstick has no blood.
White cells without growth, e.g. renal TB.
Seen in pyelonephritis and interstitial nephritis.

steps.x: **B. Oval fat bodies (lipiduria).** Nephrotic sediment: protein and fat (lipiduria). Nephritic sediment: blood and red cell casts.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has 6 weeks of leg swelling. He injects heroin and has not been tested for blood-borne viruses. His BP is 130/84 mmHg. Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 820 mg/mmol (<15) and serum albumin 16 g/L (35–50). Renal biopsy shows sclerosis affecting parts of some glomeruli.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Scarring of parts of some glomeruli is FSGS, most commonly caused by HIV, and he is at risk from injecting drugs. Membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial deposits instead.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: sclerosis affecting parts of some glomeruli
steps.x: **Segmental sclerosis** in **some** glomeruli in a man at risk of **HIV** is FSGS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FSGS.

elim: Presents with visible haematuria and mesangial IgA deposits.
Biopsy shows GBM thickening with subepithelial deposits, not segmental scarring.
Light microscopy is normal.
A nephritic picture after a throat infection.

steps.x: **A. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.** FSGS: think HIV and test with an HIV ELISA.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl has had 10 days of increasing swelling. It started around her eyes and now involves her legs and abdomen. She is not breathless. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Her serum albumin is 13 g/L (35–50).
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa
questions.e: Very low albumin causes oedema that spreads from the eyes to the legs and abdomen: ascites, found as shifting dullness. A pulsatile liver is a cardiac sign.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: started around her eyes and now involves her legs and abdomen
steps.x: Oedema spreading **periorbital to peripheral to abdomen** with very low albumin means fluid in the peritoneum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ascites: shifting dullness.

elim: Seen in tricuspid regurgitation.
Urinary retention is not a feature of nephrotic syndrome.
Suggests appendicitis.
Seen in portal hypertension or haematological disease, not nephrotic syndrome.

steps.x: **D. Shifting dullness.** Nephrotic oedema starts periorbitally and progresses to anasarca with ascites and effusions.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman has nephrotic syndrome. She has no diabetes, rash or drug history. Anti-PLA2R antibodies are negative and her HIV test is negative. Her BP is 130/80 mmHg. Investigations show urine protein:creatinine ratio 560 mg/mmol (<15), serum albumin 20 g/L (35–50) and normal renal ultrasound.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: In an adult with no clear cause, renal biopsy is the gold standard to define the histological type. Repeat quantification of protein does not give a diagnosis.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
The cause is still **unknown** after serology: she needs histology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Renal biopsy.

elim: Only quantifies proteinuria, which is already known.
Does not show glomerular histology.
Proteinuria is already quantified; it will not give the cause.
Screens for myeloma, but does not define the glomerular lesion.

steps.x: **C. Renal biopsy.** Renal biopsy is the gold standard to confirm the type of nephrotic syndrome in adults.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has 4 weeks of ankle swelling and frothy urine. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. His JVP is not raised. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. His GP sends blood tests to support a diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome.
questions.q: Which is the most likely blood test result?
questions.e: Bloods in nephrotic syndrome show low albumin and raised cholesterol. The liver makes more lipoprotein as albumin falls.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
Heavy proteinuria means albumin is lost; the liver responds by making more lipoprotein.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low albumin, high cholesterol.

elim: Cholesterol rises, not falls, in nephrotic syndrome.
Albumin would be low because it is lost in the urine.
Neither normal albumin nor hyperkalaemia is part of the triad.
A normal result does not fit nephrotic syndrome.

steps.x: **B. Albumin 15 g/L and cholesterol 9.0 mmol/L.** First-line bloods: low albumin and raised cholesterol.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has 5 weeks of leg swelling. He has had several unprotected sexual partners and recent oral candidiasis. His BP is 126/80 mmHg. Investigations show urine protein:creatinine ratio 900 mg/mmol (<15) and serum albumin 14 g/L (35–50). Renal biopsy shows focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the underlying cause?
questions.e: FSGS is most commonly caused by HIV, tested with an HIV ELISA; his sexual history and oral candidiasis support it. Anti-PLA2R is for membranous nephropathy.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
**FSGS** with risk factors and **oral candidiasis** (immunosuppression) points to HIV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HIV ELISA.

elim: Tests for membranous nephropathy, not FSGS.
Screens for lupus, which causes membranous rather than FSGS.
Diabetes is not suggested by the history.
Can cause glomerular disease, but HIV is the classic cause of FSGS and fits the candidiasis.

steps.x: **E. HIV ELISA.** FSGS: test for HIV.

questions.stem: A 62 year old White woman has 2 months of leg swelling. She has no diabetes, rash, joint pains or recent infections and takes no regular medicines. Her BP is 138/84 mmHg. Investigations show urine protein:creatinine ratio 610 mg/mmol (<15), serum albumin 19 g/L (35–50) and normal creatinine. Ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys.
questions.q: Which blood test would best support the most likely cause?
questions.e: Primary nephrotic syndrome in a White adult is most likely membranous nephropathy, which is supported by anti-PLA2R antibodies. ANCA and anti-GBM are for nephritic causes.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.

clues: no diabetes, rash, joint pains or recent infections
steps.x: A **White adult** with no secondary cause most likely has membranous nephropathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-PLA2R antibodies.

elim: Used for small vessel vasculitis with a nephritic picture.
Used for Goodpasture's disease, a nephritic pulmonary-renal syndrome.
Supports post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Not a useful test for IgA nephropathy, which is nephritic.

steps.x: **C. Anti-PLA2R antibodies.** Membranous nephropathy: anti-PLA2R antibodies.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with nephrotic syndrome has sudden breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain this morning. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her chest is clear. Her eGFR is 82 mL/min/1.73m² and chest X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Nephrotic syndrome is hypercoagulable, so sudden breathlessness is PE until proven otherwise; with normal renal function and chest X-ray, CTPA confirms it. A D-dimer is not enough when probability is high.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
**Sudden** pleuritic breathlessness and hypoxia with a **normal chest X-ray** in a hypercoagulable patient is PE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CTPA.

elim: She has a high pre-test probability; a D-dimer will not exclude PE and is raised in many illnesses.
Can show right heart strain but does not confirm PE.
Can find a DVT but does not answer the question of PE directly.
There are no features of infection.

steps.x: **A. CT pulmonary angiogram.** Breathlessness in nephrotic syndrome: urgently exclude PE.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with type 2 diabetes has his annual review. He has no oedema. His BP is 142/86 mmHg. A urine dipstick shows protein 1+ and no blood. His GP wants to quantify the protein loss to monitor his kidneys.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Dipstick screens for protein; the amount is quantified with a urine ACR, the preferred test in diabetes. A repeat dipstick is only semi-quantitative.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer, then pick the one that answers it best.
Dipstick is a **screen**; he needs a **quantitative** spot urine test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urine ACR.

elim: Not needed to quantify proteinuria in diabetes.
Shows kidney size, not the amount of protein in the urine.
Only semi-quantitative.
Shows the effect of protein loss, not how much is lost.

steps.x: **E. Urine albumin:creatinine ratio.** Dipstick screens for protein; protein:creatinine ratio or ACR quantifies it.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with membranous nephropathy has worsening oedema to the thighs and has gained 7 kg. She is already on ramipril. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg. Her JVP is not raised. Her serum albumin is 18 g/L (35–50) and creatinine 82 µmol/L (45–90).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for her oedema?
questions.e: Oedema in nephrotic syndrome is treated with a loop diuretic such as furosemide, with salt and fluid restriction. Albumin infusion gives only a short-lived effect.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.
She has fluid overload despite an ACE inhibitor: she needs a **loop diuretic**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Furosemide.

elim: Can itself cause ankle swelling.
Not routine; the effect is short-lived as albumin is lost again in the urine.
Used for minimal change disease, not to treat oedema.
A weak diuretic on its own, and with ramipril risks hyperkalaemia.

steps.x: **B. Furosemide.** Nephrotic oedema: loop diuretic (furosemide).

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has had nephrotic syndrome from membranous nephropathy for 4 months. He takes losartan and furosemide. His BP is 128/78 mmHg. His oedema is improving. Investigations show total cholesterol 8.6 mmol/L (<5.0), LDL 6.1 mmol/L (<3.0) and serum albumin 24 g/L (35–50).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: Hyperlipidaemia in nephrotic syndrome is treated with a statin. Ezetimibe is only an add-on.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.
Persistent **hyperlipidaemia** needs lipid-lowering treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Atorvastatin.

elim: Not first-line and with renal impairment raises myopathy risk.
An add-on if statins fail, not first-line.
Do not lower LDL meaningfully.
A weight-loss drug, not a lipid treatment.

steps.x: **A. Atorvastatin.** Nephrotic hyperlipidaemia: statin.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman with knee osteoarthritis has 5 weeks of leg swelling and frothy urine. She has taken ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for a year. Her BP is 130/80 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. Her serum albumin is 22 g/L (35–50). Autoantibodies and HIV test are negative.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: The first step is to treat the underlying cause: stop the NSAID. Switching to naproxen keeps her on an NSAID.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.

clues: ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for a year
Autoantibodies and HIV test are negative
steps.x: Regular **NSAID** use is a secondary cause: remove it first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop the ibuprofen.

elim: Only for steroid-resistant minimal change disease.
First-line for minimal change disease, not for a likely drug cause.
Not first-line; the likely cause is a drug that can be stopped.
Naproxen is also an NSAID and also causes nephrotic syndrome.

steps.x: **D. Stop ibuprofen.** Treat the underlying cause first: stop the NSAID.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with membranous nephropathy started ramipril 2 months ago to reduce his proteinuria. He now has a dry, tickly cough that keeps him awake. His chest is clear and chest X-ray is normal. His BP is 134/82 mmHg. Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 380 mg/mmol (<15).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
questions.e: ACE inhibitor cough is managed by switching to an ARB, which also reduces proteinuria. Amlodipine lowers BP but does not reduce protein loss.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.
An **ACE inhibitor cough**, but he still needs to **reduce proteinuria**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Switch to an ARB (candesartan).

elim: Lowers BP but does not reduce intraglomerular pressure or proteinuria like an ARB.
Treats the symptom but leaves the cause.
Amlodipine does not reduce proteinuria.
He still needs treatment to reduce proteinuria.

steps.x: **D. Stop ramipril and start candesartan.** Reduce proteinuria with an ACE inhibitor or ARB; if ACE cough, switch to an ARB.

questions.stem: An 8 year old boy is referred with 1 week of puffy eyes and swollen ankles after a cold. His BP is 98/60 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and no blood. His serum albumin is 16 g/L (35–50) and creatinine is normal. His paediatrician diagnoses minimal change disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Minimal change disease is treated first-line with oral prednisolone; typical children are not biopsied first. Ciclosporin is only second-line.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.
A typical **child** with **minimal change disease** responds to steroids.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral prednisolone.

elim: Only second-line, if steroid-resistant.
Reduces proteinuria but does not induce remission of minimal change disease.
Typical childhood disease is treated with steroids without biopsy.
Not first-line.

steps.x: **C. Oral prednisolone.** Minimal change: prednisolone first; ciclosporin if steroid-resistant.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has biopsy-proven minimal change disease. She completed 16 weeks of high-dose oral prednisolone but still has heavy proteinuria. Her BP is 124/78 mmHg. Investigations show urine protein:creatinine ratio 520 mg/mmol (<15), serum albumin 20 g/L (35–50) and normal creatinine.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Minimal change disease that fails an adequate prednisolone course is steroid-resistant; second-line is ciclosporin.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway, then pick the next step.
She failed an adequate course of steroids: **steroid-resistant** disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ciclosporin.

elim: Steroid-resistant disease will not respond to more steroids.
Renal function is normal.
Gives only short-lived benefit and does not treat the disease.
Not standard treatment for minimal change disease.

steps.x: **A. Ciclosporin.** Steroid-resistant minimal change disease: ciclosporin.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is admitted with nephrotic syndrome from membranous nephropathy. She has gross oedema and is mostly in bed. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. questions.stem: A 61 year old man with nephrotic syndrome was started on furosemide 80 mg twice daily 10 days ago. He now feels dizzy on standing and has lost 9 kg. o: Withhold furosemide and review fluid status

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has nephrotic syndrome. Her urine protein:creatinine ratio is 600 mg/mmol (<15) and serum albumin 17 g/L (35–50). Her dipstick shows no blood. Her registrar explains why such a large amount of protein is appearing in her urine.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her proteinuria?
o: Damage to the glomerular filtration barrier
questions.e: Damage to podocytes and/or the basement membrane lets large proteins, especially albumin, leak into the urine. Tubular failure causes only low-grade protein loss.

steps.x: **A. Damage to the glomerular filtration barrier.** Nephrotic syndrome: podocyte and/or GBM damage lets albumin through.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with nephrotic syndrome has a serum albumin of 18 g/L (35–50) and total cholesterol of 10.4 mmol/L (<5.0). He has no family history of hyperlipidaemia and his diet is healthy. His thyroid function is normal and he is not diabetic.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his raised cholesterol?
o: Reduced LDL receptor expression from hypothyroidism
questions.e: As albumin falls, the liver compensates by upregulating protein and lipoprotein synthesis, causing hyperlipidaemia. Familial disease is unlikely without a family history.

questions.stem: A 5 year old girl with minimal change disease goes into remission after 4 weeks of oral prednisolone. Her mother asks why steroids work so well. Electron microscopy of a research biopsy showed effacement of podocyte foot processes and no immune deposits.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman with membranous nephropathy has a BP of 118/72 mmHg. Her consultant starts lisinopril even though her BP is already normal. After 6 weeks her urine protein:creatinine ratio falls from 450 to 290 mg/mmol (<15) and her BP is unchanged.
